summary.text: Specializing to the prime \(p=11\), direct finite evaluation gives the weighted sum as \(44\pmod{121}\). The symbol used in the accepted statement is \((7/11)=-1\), since \(7\) is a quadratic nonresidue modulo \(11\), so its right-hand side is \(11(21(-1)+16)\equiv66\pmod{121}\), contradicting the claimed congruence (and revealing the reversal from the intended \((11/7)\)).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\binom nj^2\binom{n-j}{j}^2(-16)^j
\]
and let
\[
W(N)=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(42k+37)(-1)^k a(k).
\]

The universally quantified congruence in the accepted disproof uses the auxiliary quantity
\[
\operatorname{leg\_sym\_7}(p)=\left(\frac{7}{p}\right),
\]
i.e. the Legendre symbol whose modulus is the prime \(p\). Thus, despite the suggestive name and the displayed prose accompanying the statement, the precise assertion being refuted is
\[
W(p)\equiv p\left(21\left(\frac{7}{p}\right)+16\right)\pmod{p^2}
\tag{1}
\]
for every prime \(p\ne7\).

We disprove (1) by taking \(p=11\). Clearly \(11\) is prime and \(11\ne7\), so it satisfies all the hypotheses.

First compute the sequence values needed for \(W(11)\). Direct substitution into the defining finite binomial sum gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|r}
 n&a(n)\\ \hline
0&1\\
1&1\\
2&-63\\
3&-575\\
4&6913\\
5&224001\\
6&420801\\
7&-69020223\\
8&-918270975\\
9&14596918273\\
10&511845045697
\end{array}
\]
For example,
\[
a(2)=\binom20^2\binom20^2+
\binom21^2\binom11^2(-16)+
\binom22^2\binom02^2(-16)^2
=1+4(-16)+0=-63.
\]
All the other rows are obtained in exactly the same way, summing the terms for \(0\le j\le n\); terms with \(j>n-j\) vanish because \(\binom{n-j}{j}=0\).

For completeness, multiplying each of these values by its weight \((42k+37)(-1)^k\) gives the following complete calculation. The last column records the residue modulo \(11^2=121\).
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r|r}
k&a(k)&(42k+37)(-1)^k a(k)&\text{residue modulo }121\\ \hline
0&1&37&37\\
1&1&-79&42\\
2&-63&-7623&0\\
3&-575&93725&71\\
4&6913&1417165&13\\
5&224001&-55328247&92\\
6&420801&121611489&76\\
7&-69020223&22845693813&107\\
8&-918270975&-342515073675&94\\
9&14596918273&-6057721083295&31\\
10&511845045697&233913185883529&86
\end{array}
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
W(11)
&=37-79-7623+93725+1417165-55328247\\
&\quad+121611489+22845693813-342515073675\\
&\quad-6057721083295+233913185883529\\
&=227535863206839.
\end{aligned}
\]
Equivalently, adding the residues in the last column yields
\[
37+42+0+71+13+92+76+107+94+31+86=649=5\cdot121+44.
\]
Thus
\[
W(11)\equiv44\pmod{121}.
\tag{2}
\]

It remains to evaluate the Legendre symbol occurring in (1). The quadratic residues modulo \(11\) are obtained by squaring \(0,1,2,3,4,5\):
\[
0^2\equiv0,\quad1^2\equiv1,\quad2^2\equiv4,\quad
3^2\equiv9,\quad4^2\equiv5,\quad5^2\equiv3\pmod{11}.
\]
Hence the complete set of quadratic residues modulo \(11\) is
\(\{0,1,3,4,5,9\}\). Since \(7\) is not in this set and is not divisible by \(11\),
\[
\left(\frac7{11}\right)=-1.
\]
The proposed right-hand side at \(p=11\) is therefore
\[
11\left(21\left(\frac7{11}\right)+16\right)
=11(-21+16)=-55.
\]
Modulo \(121\), this is
\[
-55\equiv66\pmod{121}.
\tag{3}
\]
The residues in (2) and (3) are different: \(44\ne66\). Equivalently, their difference is
\[
44-66=-22,
\]
which is not divisible by \(121\). Therefore
\[
W(11)\not\equiv11\left(21\left(\frac7{11}\right)+16\right)\pmod{11^2}.
\]
Since \(11\) is an admissible prime, this single counterexample disproves the universal assertion (1).

There is an important notational distinction between this accepted disproof and the canonical OEIS conjecture as written in the question. The canonical conjecture contains \(\left(\frac p7\right)\), not \(\left(\frac7p\right)\). At \(p=11\), these two symbols differ. Indeed,
\[
\left(\frac{11}{7}\right)=\left(\frac47\right)=1
\]
because \(4\equiv2^2\pmod7\), whereas, as shown above, \(\left(\frac7{11}\right)=-1\). If the canonical symbol \(\left(\frac p7\right)\) is used, its right-hand side at \(p=11\) is instead
\[
11(21\cdot1+16)=11\cdot37=407\equiv44\pmod{121},
\]
which agrees with (2). Thus \(p=11\) is a counterexample to the precise statement accepted in the supplied file, because that statement defines its symbol as \(\left(\frac7p\right)\); it is not a counterexample to the canonical OEIS congruence with \(\left(\frac p7\right)\). The disproof exposes this reversal of the Legendre-symbol arguments.
